source.title: Scaling Neural Network Quantum States for Ab Initio Quantum Chemistry
source.authors: Chen Yu; Han-Lin Kong; Jia-Nan Wei; Li-Zhong Fu; Hong-Hui Shang; Wen-Guan Wang; Jin-Long Yang

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplement are present. Some equations and symbols have PDF-text encoding artifacts, but the results remain readable.
record.tranche_reason: It extends empirical scaling analysis to autoregressive neural-network quantum states for quantum chemistry, using energy error rather than language-model cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The paper reports NNQS energy-error scaling and compute-frontier results. Language-model scaling results are cited as background only. This study does not measure held-out language-model cross-entropy or vary training-token counts.
record.test_reason: It fits power laws of energy error against parameters, optimization steps and a compute proxy for autoregressive Transformer neural quantum states. This is a new, non-text training regime, and it bears directly on whether the power-law form carries over (V5). Its benchmark- and step-dependent exponents and its broken-power frontier also bear on V7. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that energy error depends jointly on model size and optimization steps, which they capture with an interaction power law. They find that compute-optimal configurations vary with budget and benchmark, so no fixed allocation rule holds. Favorable size scaling persists when fine-tuning from pretrained weights on held-out N2 but not from scratch. They stress that these are finite-range empirical descriptions, not asymptotic laws, and that the one-molecule transfer result is not a general transfer scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses autoregressive Transformer NNQSs and variational energy error in quantum chemistry, not language models and held-out cross-entropy. It varies model size and optimization steps and estimates compute with a workload-based proxy; it does not vary training-token volume.
record.method_sensitivity: Results differ between Easy and Hard benchmarks: the fitted interaction coefficients and compute-frontier forms differ. Fine-tuning size trends also depend on initialization (pretrained versus random).

fits_no_version.finding: The Pareto-optimal model size versus optimization-steps allocation shifts with budget and benchmark. Small models dominate at low compute, and larger models enter the frontier only once enough optimization is affordable. No stable power-law allocation rule is fitted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In non-LM iterative-optimization regimes (VMC), the compute-optimal split between model size and optimization steps is budget- and data-dependent, not a fixed power of compute.

record.problems: The compute measure is a hardware-independent proxy, not a complete end-to-end FLOP count. The authors call the fits finite-range and descriptive; milestones share training trajectories. Transfer evidence is restricted to one held-out molecule, and the scratch fit has low fit quality.
record.rows_left_out: The 80 individual benchmark-level MAE values across model sizes and milestones in Figure 1 are not separately extracted; the fit summaries and reported exponent changes are retained instead. Molecule-resolved curves in Supplementary Figure S2 are also not transcribed as individual rows.

untested.parts: No language-model held-out cross-entropy, and no token or data axis.
No extrapolation from small runs to runs orders of magnitude larger. The grouped CV is only within-range interpolation (0.1M–13.8M parameters).
No parameter- or token-versus-compute exponents for LMs. The Pareto allocation of size versus steps is not fitted as a power of compute.
Width and depth vary only together with parameter count. There is no fixed-size shape comparison.
Only NNQS variational energy error on small STO-3G molecules is studied, with transfer to a single held-out molecule. No image/video or repeated-data settings; no data-size axis.
No variation of parameter-counting convention, LR schedule (constant only) or fitting method across published LM laws.

missing.what: Optimization-step exponents α_S(P) at fixed model size vary non-monotonically across sizes, reaching 2.859 (Easy) and 1.131 (Hard) at the largest size.
Interaction-model coefficients: Easy a=0.0618, b=1.164, L0=17.56 mHa; Hard a=0.3367, b=0.7826, L0=13.66 mHa. The size main effect is very weak on Easy.
Ranking inversions at fixed steps, e.g. the Easy 3.5M model is best at 10K steps and 5.8M trails smaller models at 20K–30K (benchmark-level MAE grid).

record.verdict_notes: Linking to V7 is a judgment call. The setting is NNQS, not language models, so the V7 support concerns fit-dependence in general (data/benchmark, step, curve shape), not disagreement among published LM laws. Compute is a hardware-independent proxy (C = P(8Ω + 12S)). Milestones share trajectories, so the AICc and CV comparisons are descriptive. There is no data or token axis. Fine-tuning uses a fixed 10K-step budget, so the scratch result likely reflects an optimization bottleneck.

versions.untested_parts: It measures variational energy error for NNQSs, not held-out language-model cross-entropy or language-model parameter, token, and compute scaling.
It does not fit on small runs and test predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger.
It examines model parameters and optimization steps under a compute proxy, but not parameter and token counts as functions of compute or the Kaplan/Hoffmann allocation claims.
The model family varies width and depth, but the paper does not compare architectures at a fixed parameter count to test whether architecture changes loss only slightly.
The study covers NNQS energy error in quantum chemistry and fine-tuning on one held-out N2 Hamiltonian only. It does not test image/video models, repeated data, or other transfer settings.
It does not test downstream task performance as a function of pretraining loss or scale.

It reports benchmark-dependent fits and different frontier shapes, but does not systematically vary parameter-count conventions or training schedules, or establish disagreement among published language-model laws.

rows.subject: QiankunNet
rows.size_stated: Eight model sizes, approximately 0.1M to 13.8M parameters
rows.operation_detail: Fit separable, interaction, and quadratic log-response models to benchmark energy MAE across model sizes and optimization milestones.
rows.measure: Interaction scaling fit and model comparison for energy MAE
rows.baseline: Separable power law and quadratic log-response surface
rows.value: Interaction coefficient η=0.3777; R²log=0.829; AICc=-49.70 versus -35.09 for the separable model and -45.82 for the quadratic model; CV-P=0.629 and CV-S=0.478
rows.locator: Supplementary Sections S4, Table S3 and Table S4
rows.note: The interaction power law is preferred by AICc; the paper interprets positive interaction as a stronger model-size advantage with more optimization. Comparisons are described as descriptive because milestones share training trajectories.
rows.check: For V5, the Easy grid is not well described by a separable power law (R²log 0.737). An interaction term is needed (R²log 0.829), so the plain power-law form holds only partially. Values are correct.

source_check.locator_found: Supplementary S4, Tables S3–S4: Easy interaction η=0.3777, R²log=0.829, AICc=-49.70; separable AICc=-35.09.
